title: 1:1 with Priya

summary.overview: Jordan and Priya covered workload, career growth, and team health in their regular 1:1. Priya feels stretched across incident response and roadmap work and asked for a clearer on-call rotation. She is interested in growing toward a staff engineer path and in mentoring Liam. Jordan agreed to propose a rotation, set up a growth plan, and look into conference budget. They also discussed the tension between shipping speed and code review quality.

bullets.at: a third of my time went into incidents

bullets.at: A simple weekly rotation across the backend team

bullets.text: Marcus becomes backup for the notification service until the rotation exists.

bullets.at: I think I want to go for a staff engineer role

bullets.text: Proposed rule: pull requests under about 200 lines get a first review within one working day.

action_items.text: Draft a proposal for an on-call rotation across the backend team
Write a staff-level growth plan with two stretch projects

transcript.summary: Priya said a third of her time went to incidents and questions about them, including two out-of-hours responses, because she knows the notification service best and there is no rotation. Jordan took ownership of fixing the setup.

points.text: Incidents were invisible to the team; fast fixes made it look easier than it is.
points.at: I made it look easier than it is

points.text: Interim step: name Marcus as backup for the notification service.
Priya will hand off the notification runbook so it is not only in her head.

transcript: Hey Priya, thanks for making time. Let's start with how you're doing, not the project status. How have the last couple of weeks felt?
Honestly a bit tiring. The work itself is good, but I've been the person people ping whenever something breaks, and it's making it hard to focus on the planned projects.
That makes sense. Can you give me a sense of how much time it's taking? Even a rough estimate is useful.

Last week I think about a third of my time went into incidents or questions about incidents. Two of them happened outside working hours, and I ended up being the one who responded because I know the notification service best.
Did anyone else on the team notice the load, or did it mostly stay invisible?
Mostly invisible. People see me fix it quickly and assume it's no big deal. I think I made it look easier than it is, which is partly why it keeps landing on me.
That's a lot, and it isn't sustainable. I didn't realize you were carrying that much of it. Why do you think it falls to you?
Because there's no rotation. People just message me, and I don't feel I can say no when I know the answer. Marcus and Liam are capable, but they haven't been put in that role officially.
Would you be okay with me explicitly assigning a backup for the notification service for the time being, even before the rotation exists?
Yes, that would help right away. Marcus is the obvious choice because he's already touched the delivery code, and he's been asking for more ownership anyway.
Then that's on me to fix, not on you to push back. What would a good setup look like from your perspective?
A simple weekly rotation across the backend team, with a short runbook for the common problems. And a rule that if you're on call out of hours, you get a recovery day afterward.
I like all of that. I'll write up a proposal this week and run it by Marcus and the team before we make it official. I'd also want to check how it affects the contractor agreements.
Thanks, that would take a big weight off. In the meantime I'll keep covering, but I'd like to hand off the notification runbook to Marcus so it's not all in my head.

transcript.summary: Priya wants to grow toward staff engineer rather than management. The gap is scope across teams, and Jordan suggested the data pipeline redesign as proof; Priya will write a growth plan with stretch projects, due in two weeks.

points.text: Existing evidence: the release rollback checklist and the load-testing setup shared with frontend.
Jordan will share the plan with Hannah before the next calibration.
First draft of the growth plan is due in two weeks.

transcript: Okay, let's move to growth. Last time you mentioned you were thinking about what comes next. Has that become any clearer?
Yes, I think I want to go for a staff engineer role rather than into management. I enjoy the technical design work and mentoring far more than I enjoy planning meetings.
That's a really clear answer. What do you think is missing, in terms of what a staff engineer does here that you haven't had a chance to do yet?

Mostly scope. I've led the notification project, but a staff engineer would drive something that spans multiple teams, like the platform work or the data pipeline redesign. I haven't had the chance to own something that big.

That's fair feedback, and I think scope is also about influence. A staff engineer changes how the team works, not just what the team ships. Is there anything like that you've already done that we could point to?
The rollback checklist for releases, I think. I wrote it after the bad deploy in the spring and now every release uses it. And the load-testing setup that I shared with the frontend team.
Those are good examples. Add them to the growth plan. Sometimes the evidence is already there and just hasn't been written down.

Both of those are coming up in the next two quarters. If you want it, the pipeline redesign could be yours. It would involve the data team, and the design doc would be a good proof point for the promotion discussion.
I'd love that. Would it be reasonable for me to write up a growth plan with the stretch projects and the skills I'm still building, so we have something concrete to measure against?
That's exactly what I was going to suggest. Draft it, send it to me, and we'll refine it together. Then I can share it with Hannah to get her support before the next calibration.
Great. I'll aim to have a first version in two weeks.

transcript.summary: Priya will run a weekly mentoring slot with Liam, who is strong at implementation but quiet in design discussions. On code review, slow reviews and rushed approvals share one root cause, so Priya will write a short proposal for the Friday retro.

points.text: Liam hesitates to challenge ideas; Priya will review his design docs before they go wider.
Jordan will protect the mentoring time on the calendar.
Larger pull requests should be split or have a design discussion first.
points.at: anything larger needs to be split

transcript: On mentoring, Liam mentioned that he'd value some time with you. He's been quiet in design discussions and I think he'd benefit from more exposure.

I've noticed that too. He's great at implementation but hesitant to challenge ideas. I'd be happy to set up a weekly thirty-minute slot, and I could use it to review his design docs before they go to the wider team.
That's perfect, and it feeds into your growth plan as evidence of mentoring. Let's make it a recurring commitment rather than ad hoc.
Agreed. I'll send him an invite today.
Is there anything you'd want from me to make that mentoring successful? I can protect the time on the calendar, or sit in on the first session if that would help.
Just protect the time. If I know it's not going to get bumped for sprint work, I'll prepare properly. I'll ask him what he wants to work on first, so it's his agenda and not mine.
Now something I want to ask about is code review. I've heard people say reviews are getting slower, and also that some reviews get approved too quickly. What are you seeing?

Both, unfortunately. Some pull requests sit for two days because everyone's busy, and others get a quick approval because the reviewer is tired of waiting. It's the same root cause, which is too little review time and no agreement about expectations.
What do you think would help? I don't want to add heavy process.

A lightweight rule. Pull requests under about two hundred lines get a first review within one working day, and anything larger needs to be split or have a design discussion first. That would reduce both problems.
I like it. Let's bring it to the team retro on Friday and see if people agree. If so, we write it into our working agreements.
I'll write the one-paragraph proposal so we're discussing something specific. Retros go in circles when the idea is vague.
Agreed. If it helps, send it to me tonight and I'll add a line about how we'll measure whether review times actually improve.

transcript.summary: Priya would like to attend a spring backend conference and present on the notification migration; Jordan will check the budget. She is out the last week of the month, which is why the rotation matters. Her main ask of Jordan is to keep naming what gets dropped when priorities change.

points.text: Priya takes the last week of the month off; handoffs will be done before she leaves.
points.at: last week of the month off

points.text: Ask: keep telling the team what to drop when something new comes in.
points.at: what to drop when something new comes in

transcript: One more thing. There's a backend conference in the spring that I'd like to attend, and I'd be willing to present a talk about the notification migration if they accept it.
That's a great idea, and it would be good visibility for the company too. I'll check the budget this week. I think we have an allowance, but I don't know how much has already been used.
Thank you. Also I'm taking the last week of the month off, so I'll make sure the handoffs are done before I leave.
Great, and make sure you actually disconnect. With the new rotation proposal, that week is exactly why we need it. Anything else you want to cover before we wrap up?
No, I feel much better about everything. It helps to know that the rotation is being taken seriously.
I'm glad. One last thing, and it's more of a question. Is there something I could do differently as your manager? Even small things.
Honestly, the clearer priorities you gave in the last planning helped a lot. If you keep telling us what to drop when something new comes in, that's the biggest thing.
Understood, I'll keep doing that, and I'll call out what's being dropped explicitly.

It is. Let me recap what we agreed. I'm drafting the rotation proposal, checking the conference budget, and talking to Hannah about the growth plan once you send it. You're setting up the mentoring slot with Liam.
Yes, that's everything I have. Thanks, Jordan.
